subject: physiology
title: Blood groups and transfusion: ABO, Rh and reactions

steps.tx: In the **ABO system** group O red cells carry no A or B antigens with both antibodies in plasma and serve as universal red cell donor, while group AB carries both antigens with no antibodies and serves as universal plasma donor. Agglutinins are natural IgM, secretors spill antigens into saliva, and Bombay hh blood lacks H substance. The Rh system centres on D, positive in eighty five percent, and Duffy, Kidd and Kell alloimmunise, while Coombs testing coats cells in the direct test and screens serum in the indirect test.
steps.say: Group O is the universal red cell donor because its cells carry neither A nor B antigen, while group AB accepts all cells because its plasma carries neither antibody, exactly as the table lays out. Natural IgM antibodies, secretor status and the rare Bombay phenotype are completing the ABO story. Beyond ABO, the large D antigen defines Rh positivity in most people, and Kell, Duffy and Kidd systems matter because transfused patients can form antibodies against them.

vis.alt: Table of ABO groups with red cell antigen, plasma antibody and which red cells each can receive: A gets A and O, B gets B and O, AB gets all, O gets only O.
vis.caption: O has no antigens (universal red cell donor); AB has no antibodies (universal recipient).

steps.tx: **Haemolytic disease of the newborn** follows RhD negative mothers sensitised by fetomaternal bleeding or abortion, prevented by anti-D at twenty eight weeks and after delivery, quantified by the Kleihauer test, and monitored by hydrops signs and middle cerebral artery Dopplers with intrauterine transfusion when severe. ABO disease with group O mothers and A or B babies stays milder with a positive direct antiglobulin test and phototherapy. Antibody screens each pregnancy, titres near sixteen watch critically, and paternal zygosity predicts fetal risk.
steps.say: A RhD negative mother can be sensitised when fetal cells enter her circulation, then harm a later RhD positive baby as her IgG crosses the placenta, the sequence drawn in the figure. Anti-D immunoglobulin at twenty eight weeks and within seventy two hours of any sensitising event stops her making her own antibody. Kleihauer counts the bleed, Dopplers watch fetal anaemia, and intrauterine transfusion rescues severe disease, while ABO incompatibility usually stays milder.

vis.alt: Sequence of haemolytic disease of the newborn: an RhD negative mother is sensitised by fetomaternal bleeding at delivery or a sensitising event, makes anti-D IgG, and in a later RhD positive pregnancy the antibody crosses the placenta causing haemolysis; anti-D immunoglobulin prevents sensitisation.
vis.caption: Anti-D given at 28 weeks and within 72 hours of a sensitising event prevents the mother making her own antibody.

steps.tx: The **major crossmatch** mixes donor red cells with recipient serum to find recipient antibodies, the minor crossmatch reverses the mix, and electronic issue follows a type and screen, while emergencies use O negative cells and massive transfusion may use O positive for males. Predeposit autologous and family directed donations exist, and products issue by trigger: red cells by haemoglobin, platelets by count, fresh frozen plasma by factors and cryoprecipitate by fibrinogen. Leukodepleted units cut febrile reactions and cytomegalovirus risk.
steps.say: Compatibility testing protects the recipient first: the major crossmatch shown in the diagram mixes donor cells with recipient serum, the minor test reverses the partners, and a type and screen with electronic issue covers routine surgery. True emergencies release group O negative cells without waiting. Each product has its own trigger, from haemoglobin for red cells to fibrinogen for cryoprecipitate, and leukodepletion reduces febrile reactions and viral transmission.

vis.alt: Comparison of major and minor crossmatch: major crossmatch mixes donor red cells with recipient serum to detect recipient antibodies to donor cells, minor crossmatch mixes donor serum with recipient cells; emergency uses O negative red cells.
vis.caption: Major crossmatch protects the recipient and is the one that matters; in an emergency use group O negative.

steps.tx: Stop the transfusion for **transfusion reactions** spanning febrile cytokine reactions needing antipyretics, allergic reactions needing antihistamines, anaphylaxis in IgA deficiency needing adrenaline, TRALI needing ventilation and TACO needing diuretics sitting up, and haemolytic ABO reactions with back pain and disseminated coagulation needing fluids stopped. Haemovigilance tags and traces units, looks back at donors and reports to SHOT, while iron, tranexamic acid and cell salvage spare blood, Jehovah choices are respected, and irradiated units protect the immunocompromised from graft versus host disease.
steps.say: Any fever, rash, wheeze, breathlessness or flank pain during a transfusion means stop the unit, keep venous access with saline, and recheck identity before anything else. Febrile and allergic reactions settle with antipyretics and antihistamines, anaphylaxis needs adrenaline, TRALI floods the lungs needing ventilation, and TACO overloads the circulation needing diuretics. Every event feeds haemovigilance tracing, and blood sparing with iron, tranexamic acid or salvage reduces future exposure.
